_note: Text basis for each rule. 'basis' is our paraphrase of what the source describes, not a quotation. Thresholds marked origin=literature come from these descriptions; origin=engineering_prior are our starting values and must be calibrated.

S01.cite: Huntsman RJ, Lowry NJ, Sankaran K. Nonepileptic motor phenomena in the neonate. Paediatr Child Health 2008;13(8):680-4
S01.basis: Tremor = rhythmic oscillation of equal amplitude; fine tremor >6 Hz and <3 cm, coarse tremor lower frequency and larger amplitude; jitteriness = recurrent tremor, common in healthy newborns; coarse tremor and tremor that does not settle with soothing warrant investigation.

S02.cite: Safer Care Victoria. Seizures in the neonate (clinical guidance)
S02.basis: Jitteriness: symmetrical rapid movements of hands and feet. Clonic seizures: usually one limb or one side jerking rhythmically at 1-4 per second.

S03.basis: Focal clonic seizures: slow rhythmic jerking of an extremity, about 0.5-2 jerks per second; jittery movements and benign sleep myoclonus are common mimics; myoclonic jerks are not rhythmic.

S04.cite: Starship Child Health NICU. Seizures at home (parent information sheet), 2017
S04.basis: Parents can try holding and repositioning the limb: jerking that stops is probably not a seizure; time the event and consider taking a video; a suspected seizure lasting 5 minutes or more is an emergency.

S05.cite: Contemporary Pediatrics. Infantile spasms: a frontline guide for pediatricians, 2023;40(3)
S05.basis: A spasm is brief and abrupt (generally 1-3 s) involving head, neck, trunk and/or limbs; spasms can repeat every 5-10 s in clusters over minutes; home smartphone video is very helpful; treatment delay matters.

S06.cite: MedLink Neurology. Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (2026 update)
S06.basis: Spasms are brief synchronous bilateral contractions of neck, trunk and limbs lasting up to about 5 s; clustered when the interval between spasms is under 60 s.

S07.cite: Sydney Children's Hospitals Network. Infantile spasms factsheet, 2026
S07.basis: Usually start at 3-7 months; clusters of short (1-3 s) spasms over several minutes, often when falling asleep or waking; doctors diagnose partly from parent videos.

S08.cite: Einspieler C et al. Fidgety movements - tiny in appearance, but huge in impact. J Pediatr (Rio) 2016;92(3 Suppl 1):S64-70
S08.basis: Fidgety movements: small movements of moderate speed with variable acceleration of neck, trunk and limbs in all directions; may appear from ~6 weeks; continual FMs have very short (1-2 s) pauses.

S09.basis: Cramped-synchronised GMs: rigid movements lacking fluency, limb and trunk muscles contract and relax almost simultaneously; FMs are the predominant awake pattern at 3-5 months.

S10.cite: Thelen E. Rhythmical stereotypies in normal human infants. Anim Behav 1979;27:699-715 (as summarised in Front Psychol 2022;13:896319 and Front Psychol 2017;8:1168)
S10.basis: Rhythmic kicking, waving and rocking are a normal part of infant motor development, with age-dependent peaks (e.g. rhythmic hand-banging around 6-7 months); a rhythmic bout is a movement repeated in the same form at least three times at short regular intervals.

S11.basis: ATNR: head rotation produces extension of the limbs on the face side and flexion on the occiput side; most prominent at 1-4 months and disappears by 3-9 months; retained spontaneous ATNR in high-risk infants has predictive value.

S12.cite: Reliability of still photography for measuring habitual head deviation in infants with CMT (PMID 21068640); Automatic assessment of infant face and upper-body symmetry (arXiv:2210.15022); BMJ Best Practice: congenital muscular torticollis
S12.basis: Habitual head deviation can be measured from supine photographs as the angle between the eye line and the shoulder line; in CMT the head is typically tilted to one side and rotated to the other; a head-turn preference may be noticed in the first months.

S13.cite: Children's Wisconsin. Hypotonia co-management guideline (valid through 12/2026); Hidalgo-Robles A et al. Early Hum Dev 2026;221 (scoping review, GMA/MOS in central hypotonia)
S13.basis: Frog-leg positioning when supine, or extended arms or legs at rest, gives an initial sense of hypotonia; most hypotonic infants present in the first month.

S14.cite: NICHD. Cerebral palsy: signs and symptoms (NIH factsheet)
S14.basis: Under 6 months: legs get stiff or cross when picked up. Over 6 months: hard time bringing hands together; reaching with only one hand while the other is held in a fist.

S15.cite: Verhage CH et al. Upper-limb movement in infants at risk for unilateral spastic cerebral palsy: a scoping review. Dev Med Child Neurol, online 8 May 2026
S15.basis: Asymmetry appears in spontaneous wrist/digit movements, pre-reaching and reduced contralesional hand use in infants who develop USCP; from 15 weeks of age asymmetry becomes more evident.

S16.cite: Verhage CH et al. Detecting asymmetry of upper limb activity with accelerometry in infants at risk for USCP. Phys Occup Ther Pediatr 2023
S16.basis: An asymmetry index of mean upper-limb activity was higher in infants with asymmetrical hand function, from 3 months onwards.

S17.cite: Early hand preference and infantile spasms: a case of left-sided cerebral palsy. Aust J Gen Pract 2026;55(8)
S17.basis: Hand dominance before 12 months is a red flag that warrants structured work-up.

S18.cite: Smith BA et al. Daily quantity of infant leg movement. Sensors 2015;15:19006; Deng W et al. Phys Ther 2019;99:730
S18.basis: Typically developing infants produce thousands of leg movements per day; about two days of data approximate an infant's typical daily movement rate, so single short sessions are noisy and within-infant baselines are preferable.

S19.cite: Kraft KE et al. Asymmetrical finger postures during fidgety age in the prediction of unilateral CP. Early Hum Dev, online 4 May 2026
S19.basis: Finger-posture asymmetry is studied as a predictor; COCO-17 has no finger keypoints, so MoveGrow must abstain on finger/fisting rules.
